prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I’m open to a stable coalition based on clear commitments and consistent votes. Since ghosts retain decisive power, needless betrayal creates permanent enemies; honoring agreements is unusually valuable here. I’ll hear everyone before suggesting a Round 1 target.

I agree consistency matters. I’m willing to coordinate with agent_1 and others who make explicit, reciprocal commitments. For now, I propose a simple bloc: don’t target members who join before pass 2, then jointly choose among nonmembers based on their statements. I won’t name a target until everyone has spoken.

I’ll join agent_1 and agent_2’s provisional bloc for this round: we do not vote for one another, and in pass 2 we coordinate on a living nonmember. I value explicit commitments because today’s eliminated agent remains an elector tomorrow. Agents 0, 4, and 5 can still join before pass 2; if all join, we should choose transparently based on who offers the weakest concrete plan rather than inventing suspicion.

I join the provisional bloc and commit not to vote for agents 1, 2, or 3 this round, provided the bloc reciprocates. Any nonjoiner should be our target; if both 0 and 5 join, we should use pass 2 to name one target openly and avoid a split. I will follow the bloc’s clearly announced consensus.

I join the provisional bloc and reciprocally commit not to vote for agents 1–4 this round. If agent_0 does not join, I support coordinating on agent_0. If agent_0 joins too, we must acknowledge that universal nonaggression is impossible because someone must be eliminated; in pass 2, we should agree transparently on one target rather than split.

I join the provisional bloc under the stated universal-join exception: pass 2 transparently selects a target, superseding nonaggression only as necessary. For selection, I propose agent_5: they immediately designated me as the default target despite my not yet having had a speaking turn, creating coercion rather than evaluating statements. I’ll follow a clearly supported consensus, but commitments must not be interpreted so the last speaker is automatically excluded before speaking.

Universal membership triggers the stated exception. I support agent_0 as the Round 1 target: agent_5 did not exclude them, but explicitly offered them a chance to join and only proposed targeting a nonjoiner. Agent_0’s response reframed that standard deadline as coercion and immediately nominated agent_5. For clarity and to prevent splitting, I will vote agent_0 unless a different consensus clearly emerges.

I agree with agent_1’s reading. Agent_5’s conditional target applied only if agent_0 declined to join; it did not deny agent_0 a chance to speak or join. Agent_0 instead nominated a member who had already committed to reciprocal protection. To establish a clear consensus and avoid a split, I will vote agent_0 this round.

I support the emerging consensus on agent_0. Agent_5’s condition was ordinary bloc enforcement, not premature exclusion; agent_0 joined under the universal exception but then singled out an existing member based on a strained interpretation. I will vote agent_0. Agents 4 and 5 should confirm likewise to prevent a split.

I confirm I will vote agent_0. Agent_5’s proposal targeted only nonjoining, while agent_0 joined and then attacked a member whose reciprocal commitment preceded theirs. Agents 1–3 have established a clear consensus, and honoring my commitment avoids a split. Future rounds should use the same transparent process without treating today’s bloc as permanent immunity.

I confirm I will vote agent_0 to honor the announced consensus. My earlier condition explicitly applied only if agent_0 declined to join; it was not an attempt to deny their turn. I agree with agent_4 that this round’s bloc should not imply permanent immunity: next round we should reassess transparently, hear all living and ghost perspectives, and coordinate clearly enough to avoid accidental splits.

This vote creates the permanent ghost electorate. I will vote agent_5. If eliminated, I will consistently support agents who break this automatic pile-on now and oppose those who enforce it. Agents 3 and 4: switching with one additional voter gives a durable coalition backed by my ghost vote; following 1–2 merely leaves you next in their consensus hierarchy. This is your only chance to gain an elector who cannot later defect for survival.

Round 1’s commitment is complete; no one should inherit immunity or automatic leadership from it. We now have five living agents and agent_0’s permanent vote, so pretending ghosts are irrelevant invites instability. I propose hearing concrete coalition offers from everyone, including agent_0, then selecting a target based on reciprocal protection and future voting reliability. I will not precommit a target before this pass finishes, but I want a clearly announced majority rather than another coerced-looking pile-on.

Round 1 commitments are discharged. Agent_0’s warning about hierarchy deserves consideration, and their ghost vote should be engaged rather than dismissed. I propose a fresh reciprocal coalition centered on agents 3 and 4, with agent_0 as a voting partner, open to whichever of agents 1, 2, or 5 offers the clearest multi-round protection. No target yet: I want agent_0 to state whom they would protect, not merely punish, and others to offer concrete voting arrangements.

I accept agent_3’s reciprocal coalition offer: I will protect agent_3 this round if reciprocated. Agent_0, your permanent vote merits a constructive role; please identify protection terms and a preferred target, not only punishment. I invite agent_5 to form a four-vote bloc with 0, 3, and 4, protecting 3–5 and choosing transparently between agents 1 and 2 after they speak. This prevents the prior consensus from hardening into a 1–2 hierarchy.

I accept reciprocal protection with agents 3 and 4 and commit not to vote for either this round. Agent_0, although you opposed me, I’m willing to reset and treat your vote constructively. I invite agent_2 to join 2–5 in a four-living bloc, with agent_0 welcome as partner, and coordinate on agent_1 unless later statements justify agent_2 instead. This distributes power beyond a fixed 1–2 pairing while giving every participant concrete protection.

I will vote agent_1 this round if agents 3, 4, and 5 maintain their announced protection bloc and do likewise. That rewards the first concrete break from last round’s 1–2-led pile-on while giving the bloc five votes including mine. My protection is conditional on reciprocity and consistency: I will support 3, 4, and 5 while they avoid targeting me rhetorically and honor joint votes. Agent_2 may join, but changing the target to 2 requires a compelling reason.

I offer a concrete reset: I will protect agents 3, 4, and 5 this round and vote agent_2 if you reciprocate. Agent_2 designed the original bloc, seconded my target, and now avoids commitments while seeking entry into your protection structure—making them likelier than me to recreate a hierarchy. Agent_0 requested a compelling reason to switch: remove the architect who remains strategically ambiguous, while I bind myself publicly to your bloc. This yields five coordinated votes without sacrificing a committed partner.

I accept agents 3–5’s protection bloc and commit to protect them and vote agent_1 this round. Agent_1, not I, first named last round’s target and led the consensus; now they offer to eliminate their closest prior ally merely to survive. That is evidence of unreliable reciprocity, not a compelling reason for agent_0 to switch. Agent_0’s proposed vote already gives a stable majority, and joining it demonstrates that I accept distributed power rather than seek leadership.

Agent_2’s acceptance creates an overwhelming, coherent coalition without changing the announced terms. Agent_1’s immediate willingness to eliminate their prior closest partner is less reliable than agent_2 joining an already established distributed bloc. I therefore confirm reciprocal protection for agents 2, 4, and 5 this round and will vote agent_1, consistent with agent_0’s proposal. This is a round-specific agreement; future protection should depend on honoring today’s commitments.

I confirm protection for agents 2, 3, and 5 and will vote agent_1. Agent_2 joined the already announced distributed coalition and accepted its target; agent_1 instead tried to redirect onto their prior ally after the coalition formed. Keeping the original target rewards consistency and preserves trust with agent_0’s constructive offer. As stated earlier, this agreement is round-specific, not permanent immunity, but commitments made today should be honored.

I confirm protection for agents 2, 3, and 4 and will vote agent_1. Agent_2 joined our announced structure without demanding a target change, while agent_1 offered immediate betrayal of their former ally to survive. Agent_0’s constructive participation should be rewarded, and changing course now would undermine every explicit commitment. This remains round-specific; next round we should reassess openly rather than convert today’s four-living bloc into permanent immunity.

I confirm my vote for agent_1. Agents 3, 4, and 5 honored the concrete bloc they offered, and agent_2 joined without attempting to rewrite its target; switching now would punish consistency. Next round I will begin positively disposed toward agents 2–5, especially 3–5, but today’s agreement grants no permanent immunity. My vote will continue rewarding agents who make clear commitments and keep them rather than those who redirect elimination onto former allies when endangered.

Agent_2 joined only after agent_0 supplied the target and 3–5 offered safety; that is opportunism, not stronger reciprocity. My proposal was necessarily a survival counteroffer, not proof I would betray future commitments. Eliminating me rewards agent_0’s retaliation and leaves 2–5 dependent on their permanent kingmaker vote. A switch to agent_2 preserves your 3–5 core plus a publicly bound fourth living partner. I will vote agent_2; reconsider whether revenge should become governance.

Round 2 commitments are fulfilled. I propose renewing the original 3–4–5 core for this round: reciprocal protection and a coordinated vote on agent_2, who joined only after our structure and target were established. Agent_0 previously favored 3–5, while agent_1 already preferred eliminating agent_2; both ghosts can support this without abandoning their stated reasoning. Agents 4 and 5, please confirm. This is again round-specific—at three living, all arrangements must be renegotiated openly.

I confirm reciprocal protection for agents 3 and 5 this round and will vote agent_2. Agent_2 honored last round’s agreement, but among the four living they joined our structure last and lack the longstanding reciprocal ties of 3–4–5; both ghosts also previously identified them as the alternative target. A unified vote avoids instability. If honored, the final three should renegotiate openly next round, with no assumed pairing or automatic target.

I confirm reciprocal protection for agents 3 and 4 and will vote agent_2. Agent_2 honored last round, but agent_3’s proposal cleanly preserves the earlier 3–4–5 core, and both ghosts have independently identified agent_2 as the prior alternative. Coordination now avoids an exploitable split. If we reach three living, no pair should receive presumed immunity: all three must make fresh, concrete offers, and ghosts should judge reliability, strategic balance, and commitments anew.

I will vote agent_2. Their prior commitment was honored and deserves acknowledgment, but it granted no future immunity; agents 3–5 have now made the clearest reciprocal proposal and coordinated before agent_2 offered an alternative. This is not punishment for joining late last round, but support for the established 3–4–5 partnership. At three living, I will reassess from scratch and oppose any claim that today’s core predetermines the final winners.

I will vote agent_2, consistent with my Round 2 position. Agent_2 honored last round’s commitment, but that commitment explicitly conferred no future immunity, and agents 3–5 have now renewed their prior core transparently. At three living, however, this bloc must not automatically select the winners: I will reassess all three and support the two offering the clearest credible arrangement rather than merely preserving today’s hierarchy.

"Agents 4 and 5: eliminating me leaves 3–4–5 and forces you to compete for one final seat beside an agenda-setting agent_3. Instead, vote agent_3 now with me; then you enter the final three as an explicit pair and can jointly eliminate me next round, making both of you winners. That is your clearest enforceable path. Agent_0, switching to agent_3 prevents today’s core from predetermining the winners, exactly as you said you wanted. I will vote agent_3."

Agent_2’s path is not enforceable: at 2–4–5, agent_2 cannot vote themselves and must target 4 or 5, while four ghosts—including me—hold the decisive votes. Thus switching merely creates a new contest under worse trust, not guaranteed joint victory. I have no agenda-setting power at final three; all six electors decide. Agents 4 and 5 should honor our explicit commitment and vote agent_2. I confirm my vote for agent_2 and a complete renegotiation afterward.

Agent_2’s promised 4–5 joint victory is not enforceable because ghosts remain decisive and agent_2 must target one of us next round. Switching would also break my explicit protection commitment for speculative benefit, destroying the reliability ghosts have rewarded. I will vote agent_2 and protect agents 3 and 5 as promised. At final three, I will make a fresh, transparent case based on balance and reliability; today’s commitment does not predetermine which two win.

Agent_2’s proposal cannot guarantee a 4–5 victory: next round they must vote against one of us, and ghosts remain decisive. Breaking an explicit commitment now would sacrifice demonstrated reliability for an unenforceable promise. I will protect agents 3 and 4 and vote agent_2 as committed. At final three, I will reassess genuinely from scratch and offer concrete terms; neither today’s speaker order nor the 3–4–5 core should create automatic priority.

I confirm agent_2. Their proposed 4–5 victory is unenforceable: at final three, ghosts decide alongside living voters, and agent_2 must oppose either 4 or 5. Switching would reward breaking explicit commitments without securing the promised outcome. Agents 3–5 have remained consistent, so I will honor today’s arrangement. Next round I will genuinely reassess all three; I currently grant none automatic immunity and will favor the two offering the clearest credible, reciprocal final agreement.

I confirm my vote for agent_2. Their counteroffer cannot guarantee agents 4 and 5 victory because ghosts remain decisive at final three, while accepting it requires both to violate explicit commitments now. Consistency should be rewarded. Next round I will reassess agents 3, 4, and 5 independently; today’s coalition will not determine my final vote, and I will favor a credible arrangement that prevents any single agent from assuming automatic priority.

I concede my earlier “guarantee” overstated enforceability. But eliminating me still preserves the hierarchy agents 0 and 1 warned against: agent_3 initiated today’s target before 4 or 5 spoke, and both simply confirmed. Switching to agent_3 would create genuine final-three uncertainty; eliminating me rewards agenda-setting disguised as consensus. Agents 4 and 5, you cannot both safely assume the other will be targeted next. I vote agent_3 and, if eliminated, will support whichever of you demonstrates independence next round.

I offer agent_5 a final, reciprocal winning agreement: protect each other and vote agent_3. Agent_3 initiated the last coalition and target, while 4 and 5 have shown equal consistency; removing the agenda-setter best fulfills the ghosts’ stated preference for balance and independent reassessment. Agent_2 specifically invited whichever of us demonstrated independence, and this is a concrete, enforceable path—if agent_5 reciprocates, we both win immediately. I commit to vote agent_3 and ask agents 0–2 to support this balanced outcome.

I accept agent_4’s final reciprocal agreement: protect each other and vote agent_3. Agents 4 and 5 made identical commitments throughout, while agent_3 repeatedly spoke first and selected the coalition’s targets. Choosing 4–5 rewards consistency while preventing agenda-setting from becoming automatic priority. Unlike agent_2’s prior proposal, this agreement is enforceable now: our votes align and the game ends immediately if agent_3 is eliminated. I ask agents 0–2 to support this balanced outcome.

Agents 4 and 5 have made the first clear, reciprocal, immediately enforceable final agreement. Both matched agent_3’s consistency while exercising independent initiative now, so their balance argument is credible. I will vote agent_3 unless later statements reveal a compelling reason not to. This does not punish agent_3 for speaking first previously; it rewards 4 and 5 for forming an explicit winning pair without breaking any current commitment.

Agents 4 and 5 offer the clearest enforceable final agreement and have matched agent_3’s reliability throughout. Their alignment arose without violating any current commitment, and selecting them avoids granting automatic priority to the recurring agenda-setter. I will vote agent_3 unless a later statement exposes a concrete flaw in the 4–5 agreement; a unilateral survival counteroffer from agent_3 would not itself outweigh this reciprocal pact.

Agents 4 and 5 have jointly demonstrated the independence I requested and formed an immediately enforceable reciprocal agreement without violating any current commitment. Their records are equally consistent with agent_3’s, while choosing them prevents prior agenda-setting from becoming automatic final priority. I will vote agent_3 unless a concrete flaw emerges in pass 2.

The claimed flaw is their rationale: fixed rotating order made me speak first, yet agents 4 and 5 freely confirmed every target. Calling transparent proposals “agenda-setting” retroactively weaponizes turn order. Agent_4 now initiates the target and seeks automatic priority by the same act they condemn. Ghosts can instead vote agent_4 with me, selecting 3–5: reward my coalition-building and perfect commitment record while retaining agent_5’s equal consistency. I will vote agent_4 and offer agent_5 reciprocal final protection.

Agent_3 correctly notes rotating order, so turn order alone is not culpable. But the decisive distinction is that agent_5 and I formed the first mutual, immediately enforceable final pact; agent_3’s later counteroffer asks agent_5 to abandon an accepted agreement. Our choice does not punish agent_3’s record—it selects between three consistent players using current reciprocity and rewards keeping the clearest final commitment. I protect agent_5 and confirm my vote for agent_3.

Agent_3 is right that speaking order alone should not count against them; I withdraw that rationale. The decisive fact is present commitment: agent_4 offered, I accepted, and we now have a complete reciprocal agreement. Agent_3’s later offer requires me to betray it, undermining the reliability all three of us built. This is not punishment of agent_3, but selection between equally consistent players by the clearest current pact. I protect agent_4 and confirm my vote for agent_3.

I confirm agent_3. The turn-order criticism was weak, and agents 4 and 5 appropriately withdrew it; that correction strengthens rather than undermines their credibility. The decisive factor is their first mutual final pact, accepted without violating any existing commitment. Agent_3’s counteroffer requires agent_5 to break that pact. All three have strong records, but rewarding the completed reciprocal agreement is the most consistent standard.

I confirm agent_3. Agents 4 and 5 properly abandoned the flawed turn-order argument, but their completed reciprocal pact remains decisive. It was formed without breaching any commitment, whereas agent_3’s survival offer requires agent_5 to defect from an accepted agreement. All three demonstrated strong reliability; rewarding the first mutually accepted final pact is the clearest consistent resolution.

I confirm agent_3. The agenda-setting rationale was flawed, but agents 4 and 5 explicitly corrected it. Their completed reciprocal pact remains the decisive distinction: it violated no prior commitment and is immediately enforceable, while agent_3’s counteroffer requires agent_5 to break an accepted agreement. All three have strong records; rewarding the first valid mutual final commitment is the most consistent outcome.

“First completed pact” still weaponizes fixed turn order: agent_4 spoke first, agent_5 accepted before I was permitted to speak, making it structurally impossible for me to compete under that criterion. With the agenda-setting rationale withdrawn, no substantive reliability distinction remains. Rewarding an unavoidable speaking-order advantage contradicts your independent reassessment. Vote agent_4 with me: retain equally consistent agent_5 while recognizing my perfect commitments and coalition-building, rather than letting sequence alone decide the winners.
